722.title: The blind prince
722.hook: a frightened widow shuts her eyes, a prince is born blind, and the Gita's first voice arrives
722.tomorrow: a second widow, and a maid who knows how to welcome a guest.
722.howItsDone: The ancient custom in this story, called niyoga, is described in old texts and the epics; it is not practiced in Hindu families today. Many Hindus who read the Gita hear its first verse, Dhritarashtra's question about 'my sons', as the start of its teaching on moha.

segments.voice: Last week ended with Satyavati thinking of her firstborn, and Vyasa appearing at once. smarana: remembering god is itself devotion.

Vyasa comes to the palace straight from the forest, and he looks it. The text describes him: dark skin, matted hair the color of copper, a rough beard, blazing eyes, and a smell no one would call perfume. His mother has asked him to give the house of the Kurus a son. He agrees, and asks that they wait first. Satyavati answers: there is no time.
screen: `A SAGE FROM THE FOREST.` → `HE ASKS FOR TIME.` → `THERE IS NO TIME.`

segments.voice: This starts a new part: the fathers of the cousins. In those days, when a king died without sons, a learned man could be asked to father an heir in his name. Vyasa asks that the widows first keep a vow. Satyavati says the kingdom can't wait. So the elder widow, Ambika, is told someone will come tonight. The lamp is lit, in walks the sage with blazing eyes and copper hair, and she's so afraid she shuts her eyes and keeps them shut. Afterward Vyasa tells his mother: the son will be strong and wise, but because his mother closed her eyes, he'll be born blind. That son is Dhritarashtra. Here's why Hindus still know his name. Years later, the Bhagavad Gita, one of Hinduism's most loved books, opens with this blind king. He asks what happened on the battlefield, and he says: my sons, and the sons of Pandu. Many teachers stop right there. Mine, and theirs. They read his blindness two ways: his eyes, and his heart. Hindus have a word for that second blindness: moha, attachment so strong it stops you seeing clearly. It's one of six inner enemies the tradition names. And near its end, the Gita has Arjuna say his moha is gone. The whole book walks from a blind 'mine' to clear sight. Today it looks like a parent who can't see what their own kid did, or a fan who can't see their team's foul. Love isn't the problem. Love that can only say 'mine' is.
screen: `AN OLD CUSTOM FOR A LINE.` · `AMBIKA SHUTS HER EYES.` · `DHRITARASHTRA, BORN BLIND.` · `MINE, AND THEIRS.` · then, large: `MOHA: THE BLINDNESS OF 'MINE'.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you call yours: a child, a sibling, a friend, a team. Picture them clearly, the good and the not-so-good, the way an honest neighbor would see them. If you pray, hold them before God and ask to see them truly. If you don't, just let your eyes stay open to all of them. Love doesn't need you to look away.
Dhritarashtra, born blind because his frightened mother shut her eyes, and the first voice you hear in the Bhagavad Gita.

723.title: The maid who welcomed the sage
723.hook: the younger widow turns pale, the elder sends her maid instead, and the maid's welcome gives the palace its wisest son
723.carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god
723.tomorrow: a princess learns her groom is blind, and takes a vow.
723.howItsDone: Atithi devo bhava, from the Taittiriya Upanishad, is still taught to Hindu children and lived at the door: water first, the best seat, a full plate. Vidura's later counsel, the Vidura Niti, is read by some Hindus as a guide to wise living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambika shut her eyes, and Dhritarashtra was born blind. Moha: the blindness of 'mine'.

Same palace, same sage, a different widow. Satyavati sends Vyasa to the younger princess, Ambalika. When she sees him, the blood leaves her face. She doesn't shut her eyes, as her sister did; her fear shows on her face instead. And the Kuru house is about to get three brothers: the blind one, the pale one, and one nobody planned for at all.
screen: `A DIFFERENT WIDOW.` → `SHE GOES PALE.` → `ONE NOBODY PLANNED FOR.`

segments.voice: Vyasa tells his mother: because she turned pale, the son will be pale. Pandu, the pale one. Satyavati asks for one more son from the elder widow. But Ambika can't face him again. She dresses her maid in her own jewels and sends her instead. The maid isn't afraid. She rises when the sage comes in, greets him with respect, and serves him. Vyasa is pleased. You are no longer a servant, he tells her, and your son will be virtuous and wise. That son is Vidura, and the text later says he is Dharma itself, the god of what's right, born as a man. So, three brothers: one who can't see, one who's pale, and the wisest, born to the woman everyone else overlooked. Hindus have a name for what she did. Atithi devo bhava: let the guest be God to you. It comes from the Taittiriya Upanishad, part of a teacher's parting advice to students, beside honoring mother, father and teacher. The princesses saw a frightening stranger. The maid saw someone to honor, and her life changed. Many teachers read it this way: the welcome itself is worship. That's why, in many Hindu homes, a guest gets water before asking, the best seat, and the first plate, even unannounced, even when there's little to give. Today it's the friend who drops by and leaves full, or the new kid you wave over to your table. In this tradition, how you greet the one at your door is part of how you greet God.

segments.voice: Bring to mind who might come to your door this week: a friend, a neighbor, a relative you find hard. Picture greeting them the way the maid did: standing up, a glass of water, a real hello. If you pray, offer a little water or food at your altar or in your heart first, as many Hindus do before eating. If you don't, just choose one small welcome you'll give.

724.title: Gandhari's blindfold
724.hook: the pale one is crowned, and a princess learns her groom is blind and takes a vow with a strip of cloth
724.carry: a vrata: a hardship chosen for love
724.tomorrow: a king out hunting shoots a deer, and the deer speaks.
724.howItsDone: Vratas, chosen vows like a weekly fast or Karva Chauth, are kept in many Hindu homes. Gandhari is remembered in retellings as a figure of pativrata, devotion to a husband, and her blindfold is the image tellers and painters use for a vow kept for life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandu the pale, and Vidura, born to the maid who honored a guest. Atithi devo bhava: the guest is God.

A strip of cloth, folded over and over, tied behind the head. A young princess named Gandhari, from the land of Gandhara, has been promised to a prince of the Kurus. Then she learns that he is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it, and binds her own eyes. Before we get to why, see the boys grow up.
screen: `A CLOTH, FOLDED MANY TIMES.` → `A PROMISED PRINCESS.` → `SHE BINDS HER OWN EYES.`

segments.voice: First, the boys grow up. Bhishma raises them as his own. Dhritarashtra becomes the strongest, Pandu the finest archer, and Vidura knows dharma best. The eldest is blind, so the text says the crown passes to Pandu. Then Bhishma asks for Gandhari, princess of Gandhara, as Dhritarashtra's bride. Her family hesitates over a blind groom, then agrees. When Gandhari hears, she folds a cloth and binds her eyes, resolving, the text says, never to have more than her husband has. Her brother, Shakuni, brings her to Hastinapura. Remember his name. Retellings call the blindfold her vow, and Hindus have a word for a vow like that: vrata. A vrata is a hardship you choose to take on, usually for God or for someone you love: a fast, a silence, giving something up. It's one of the most common practices in Hindu homes today. Some fast on Mondays for Shiva. Many married women keep Karva Chauth, fasting from sunrise until the moon rises, praying for their husband's long life. Readers still argue about Gandhari's vow. Some see complete devotion. Some see a quiet protest at a marriage she didn't choose. Some see grief. All of them treat it as her choice, and that's the heart of a vrata: nobody can take it for you, and nobody should force it on you. Today a vrata can be small: going without something you love, on a day you pray for someone, and meaning it.

segments.voice: Pick one small thing you could go without today, a snack, your phone at dinner, one show, and one person you'll hold in mind while you do. If you pray, offer it to God for them. If you don't, let it be a quiet gift. Keep it small and kind; a vrata isn't a punishment.

725.title: Pandu and the deer
725.hook: King Pandu, out hunting, shoots a deer that turns out to be a sage, and one quick arrow bears fruit for the rest of his life
725.carry: karma: even a quick arrow bears fruit
725.tomorrow: Kunti tells Pandu a secret: words a sage gave her as a girl.
725.howItsDone: Many Hindus understand both the curse and Pandu's answer through karma, action and its fruit. Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is also an important value, and stories like Kindama's are retold to show how seriously even a lawful harm can be taken.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown went to Pandu, and Gandhari bound her eyes. A vrata: a hardship chosen for love.

A stag and a doe, together in a quiet forest clearing. A king on the hunt sees them through the trees, draws his bow, and shoots, quickly, without warning. The arrows strike the stag, and it falls. Then, lying in the grass, it speaks in a man's voice. King Pandu has just shot a sage.
screen: `A STAG AND A DOE.` → `THE ARROWS STRIKE.` → `THE DEER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Back up a little. At her self-choice, the princess Kunti chose Pandu for her husband, and Bhishma brought him a second wife, Madri. Pandu won wars, filled the treasury, then went to the forest with both wives to hunt. That's where he meets the deer. The stag is a sage named Kindama, who had taken a deer's form to be with his wife. As he dies, he says: even a king who may hunt should not strike a creature at a moment like this. You've killed me in a moment of love. So when you go to your wife in love, you will die. And Pandu has no son yet. This is karma, one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, in a single arrow. Karma means action, and every action bears fruit, sooner or later, in this life or another. Not a punishment from an angry god; more like a seed that has to grow. Pandu's arrow took an instant. Its fruit took the rest of his life. But watch what he does next, because that's karma too. He doesn't rage or hide. He grieves, gives his jewels and robes to Brahmanas, sends his attendants home, and chooses the forest life of fasting and austerity. Kunti and Madri refuse to leave him. You can't call the arrow back. You can choose the next action. Today it's the angry text you sent at midnight. Karma says it will bear fruit. It also says your next action is already a new seed.

726.title: Kunti's mantra
726.hook: in the forest, Kunti tells Pandu about a mantra a sage gave her as a girl, and three gods answer
726.carry: a mantra: sacred words that call the divine
726.tomorrow: the cousins grow up under one roof, and something else grows with them.
726.howItsDone: Many Hindus receive a mantra from a guru or an elder and repeat it daily in japa, often on a mala of 108 beads. In this story, Dharma, Vayu and Indra become fathers of the Pandava brothers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Pandu's arrow, and Kindama's shapa, the curse that left a king with no way to have sons. Karma: even a quick arrow bears fruit.

Years before any of this, a girl named Kunti served a sage in her father's house. He was Durvasa, hard to please, and she served him so carefully that, when he left, he gave her a gift: a mantra. With it she could call any god she chose, and have a son by him. She has kept it quiet ever since. Now her husband sits in the forest, cursed, asking how his line can go on.
screen: `A GIRL SERVES A SAGE.` → `A MANTRA, GIVEN.` → `KEPT QUIET FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: Pandu raises it first. He tells Kunti of the old custom, the one that brought him into the world, and asks her to have sons for him. Kunti answers with her secret: the mantra. Pandu is overjoyed. Which god first? He chooses Dharma, so the eldest will be just. Kunti speaks the mantra, Dharma comes, and Yudhishthira is born. Next, strength: she calls Vayu, the wind, and Bhima is born. As a baby he tumbles from her lap onto a mountain, and it's the rock that shatters. Then Indra, king of the gods, and Arjuna is born. Justice, strength and skill. Notice how the mantra came to her: not bought, not stolen. Given by a sage, for her service, and kept quiet for years. That's how Hindus treat mantras. Many Hindus understand a mantra as sacred sound, words that carry the presence of the one they name, which is why you hear them at pujas, weddings and morning prayers. In many families and lineages, a personal mantra is received from a teacher and kept private, said with care, never shown off. Many Hindus repeat one daily on a mala of a hundred and eight beads, a practice called japa. In the story, Kunti's words call a god and he comes. In daily practice the tradition says something gentler: say the name with your whole attention, and you turn toward the one you're calling. And notice what Kunti doesn't tell Pandu: what happened the first time she tried it. That waits a few days.

segments.voice: Try a little japa. Choose a sacred word you know: Om, or a name like Rama, Krishna or Shiva. Say it slowly eleven times, softly or in your head, counting on your fingers and giving each one your whole attention. If you don't pray, use Om simply as a sound, and listen to it fade.
Mantra, sacred sound: Kunti's, given by Durvasa, called Dharma, Vayu and Indra to father Yudhishthira, Bhima and Arjuna.

727.title: Poison at the river
727.hook: the cousins grow up under one roof, and envy grows with them until it reaches for poison
727.carry: matsarya: envy, one of the six enemies

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti's mantra called Dharma, Vayu and Indra. A mantra: sacred words that call the divine.

A fruit tree in a royal garden, boys up in its branches reaching for fruit. Below stands Bhima, the second son of Pandu. He kicks the trunk, and the boys come tumbling down with the fruit. In the water he holds his cousins under until they gasp. In the dust he drags them by the hair. The Mahabharata says he meant no malice; it was a boy's play. But one of the boys on the ground is Duryodhana, the eldest son of Dhritarashtra. And he doesn't forget.
screen: `A TREE FULL OF COUSINS.` → `BHIMA KICKS THE TRUNK.` → `DURYODHANA DOESN'T FORGET.`

segments.voice: The story moves fast now. Madri has twin sons, Nakula and Sahadeva. In Hastinapura, Gandhari's sons are born, Duryodhana the eldest. In the forest, Pandu dies. Sages bring Kunti and the five brothers to Hastinapura, and two families of cousins share one palace. Bhima beats them all, and Duryodhana, the story says, burns with jealousy. So he holds a day of water games by the Ganga, poisons Bhima's food, ties him as he sleeps, and pushes him into the river. Bhima sinks to the realm of the Nagas, the serpent people. Their bites work against the poison, the Naga king welcomes him, and he comes home stronger. Vidura tells Kunti to say nothing in public, for her other sons' sake. Hindu teachers have a name for what grew in Duryodhana. The tradition counts six inner enemies: desire, anger, greed, moha, which we met with his blind father, pride, and matsarya, envy. Matsarya is the pain of watching someone else have what you want. Notice it doesn't start as poison. It starts with a boy on the ground under a fruit tree, watching his cousin win. Fed every day, it grows into a plan. The tradition calls it an enemy because it lives inside you and fights you. Today it's a cousin's acceptance letter, a friend's post, a sibling praised at dinner. The feeling comes. The question is whether you feed it.
screen: `TWO FAMILIES, ONE PALACE.` · `POISON AT THE RIVER.` · `RESCUED AMONG THE NAGAS.` · `SIX INNER ENEMIES.` · then, large: `MATSARYA: ENVY.`

segments.voice: The Yoga Sutra, an old Hindu guide to the mind, offers a cure: meet the happy with friendliness. Bring to mind someone who has something you wanted. Notice the sting, and name it: matsarya. Then wish them well, once, plainly: may it go well for you. If you pray, ask God's blessing on them. If you don't, just let the wish stand.

728.title: Pritha calls the sun
728.hook: a girl in a king's house is given a mantra by a sage, tries it on the rising sun, and the sun answers

segments.voice: Yesterday: poison at the river, and a boy who came home stronger among the Nagas. Matsarya: envy, one of the six enemies.

Two days ago, Kunti told Pandu about a sage's mantra, and held one piece back. Today the poem steps back in time to tell it. Before Kunti was a queen, she was a girl called Pritha, raised in the house of a king named Kuntibhoja. When the sage Durvasa came as a guest, the hard work of looking after him fell to her, and she did it well. His gift was the mantra. Now she is young, unmarried, alone with words that can summon a god.
screen: `THE PIECE KUNTI HELD BACK.` → `PRITHA, IN KUNTIBHOJA'S HOUSE.` → `DURVASA'S GIFT: A MANTRA.`

segments.voice: With the mantra, Durvasa told her, she could call any god, and that god would give her a son. Then he left. And the text says that, out of curiosity, she tries it. She looks at the rising sun and speaks the words. And Surya, the sun god, comes. Pritha is frightened. She says she only wanted to see if the gift worked, and asks him to go. Surya answers that a god called by this mantra can't return for nothing. A son will be born. But he promises she'll remain a maiden, her honor kept. So before the five brothers, Kunti had a son, the son of the sun. Nobody in the palace knows. Notice who answered her. Not a far-off idea: the sun, right in front of her. Hindus have honored Surya as a god since the Vedas. One of the most famous Vedic prayers, the Gayatri mantra, is addressed to the sun as Savitr, the one who rouses. Many Hindus still begin the day facing the rising sun, offering water from a small pot, some saying the Gayatri as they pour. Others do Surya namaskar, the sun salutation. The teaching inside it: the light that wakes you, warms the earth and grows your food is a gift, and the right answer to a gift is a greeting. Pritha's story adds the warning: sacred things answer, so handle them with care. Today, it's ten seconds at a window in the morning, thanking the light before you check your phone.
screen: `SHE TRIES IT ON THE SUN.` · `A SON WILL BE BORN.` · `SURYA, HONORED SINCE THE VEDAS.` · `GAYATRI: A PRAYER TO THE SUN.` · then, large: `THE SUN, GREETED EACH MORNING.`

segments.voice: Face a window, or wherever the light comes in. Put your palms together, the way many Hindus greet the morning sun, and thank the light: for waking you, for warming the earth, for your food. If you pray, greet Surya by name. If it's morning and you have water nearby, some Hindus pour a little toward the sun as an offering. If you don't pray, just feel the light on your face.
